reason: Both sources thoroughly document the timeline, the two ship detonations, the destruction of the city fire department, and the catastrophic casualties.
story: On the morning of April 16, 1947, dockworkers in Texas City spotted smoke rising from the hold of the French freighter SS Grandcamp, loaded with tons of ammonium nitrate fertilizer. Curious spectators gathered along the waterfront while the entire Texas City Fire Department rushed to the pier. At 9:12 A.M., the ship detonated with cataclysmic force. The blast obliterated the dock area, leveled the adjacent Monsanto chemical plant, crushed neighboring oil tanks, and instantly killed the responding firefighters along with the crowd watching from the pier. All of the city's firefighting apparatus was destroyed in seconds. Shattered debris and flaming twine ignited secondary fires across more than a thousand buildings. Sixteen hours later, as volunteers and rescue teams labored in the ruins, another ammonium-nitrate-laden freighter, the SS High Flyer, exploded at 1:10 A.M., devastating the already shattered port a second time.
angle: The initial blast instantly wiped out the entire municipal fire department and all its equipment, leaving the burning city defenseless before a second ship exploded sixteen hours later.

disputed: Total fatalities: The initial April 1947 fire underwriters report counted 433 recovered bodies and 135 missing, whereas the Texas State Historical Association cites the anchor monument record of 576 known dead (398 identified and 178 missing). The script should state that early tallies counted around 568 dead and missing, while later commemorations recorded 576 dead.

Monetary property damage: Early estimates in the 1947 report listed non-marine property loss between $35 million and $40 million, whereas the historical handbook totals losses at roughly $67 million. The script should attribute these figures as estimates ranging from $35 million up to $67 million.
